title: Who emits the carbon
hook: Count carbon dioxide by country, by person or since 1850, and the ranking flips each time.
notes: All figures: Global Carbon Project, Global Carbon Budget 2025, fossil CO2 emissions dataset version 2025v15 (Andrew & Peters, Zenodo, doi 10.5281/zenodo.17417124), licensed CC BY 4.0. Emissions are from fossil fuels and cement, counted where they are produced (territorial); emissions from deforestation and other land-use change are not included, and neither are emissions embodied in imported goods. Per-person figures use the dataset's own population series. Cumulative emissions are summed from 1850 to 2024, with historical emissions assigned to today's borders (for example, Soviet-era emissions are split among Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan and the other successor states). World totals include international aviation and shipping, about 3% of the 2024 total, which no country is assigned; shares are of that world total.

scenes.title: Who emits most today
scenes.text: In 2024 the world emitted about 38.6 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels and making cement. China emitted 12.3 billion tonnes, nearly a third of the total. The United States emitted 4.9 billion and India 3.2 billion.

scenes.title: How the centre of emissions moved
scenes.text: In 1950 the United States produced 43% of the world's fossil CO2. China overtook it in 2006. US emissions peaked around 2005 and are now about a fifth lower, while China's nearly doubled again after 2006. Press Play to watch.

captions.1950: The US alone emits 43% of the world total.
captions.1991: The Soviet Union collapses; emissions in Russia and Ukraine fall steeply.
captions.2006: China overtakes the US as the largest emitter.
captions.2020: The pandemic cuts world emissions by about 5%, for one year.

scenes.title: Per person, the order flips
scenes.text: Divide by population and the map looks different. The average person in Qatar emits about 41 tonnes of CO2 a year, an American about 14, a Chinese about 9, an Indian about 2. In much of Africa it is a few hundred kilograms or less. The world average is under 5 tonnes.

scenes.title: Counting since 1850
scenes.text: Carbon dioxide stays in the air for centuries, so what has piled up matters most for warming. Since 1850 the United States has emitted about 435 billion tonnes, nearly a quarter of the total. China is second with about 15%, Russia third. India, third today, has emitted less than 4%.

chart.title: Share of all CO2 emitted since 1850

scenes.title: Three ways to count
scenes.text: The same emissions, counted three ways. Each count puts a different country on top. Pick one.

options.label: Total, 2024
options.text: By yearly total, China leads by far: 12.3 billion tonnes in 2024, more than the United States, India and Russia together.

options.label: Per person
options.text: Per person, small oil and gas producers lead: Qatar, Kuwait, Brunei, Bahrain. Among large countries, Saudi Arabia (about 20 tonnes), Australia and the US (about 14) top the list. China is far down, India further still.

options.label: Since 1850
options.text: Added up since 1850, the United States is first again, with about 24% of all fossil CO2 ever emitted. Europe's early industrial powers, Germany and Britain, still rank in the top five.
